entities.name: wreck of the RMS Titanic
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The wreck of the RMS Titanic, a luxury British ocean liner, represents one of the most infamous maritime disasters in history, occurring on April 15, 1912, when the vessel sank after colliding with an iceberg during its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York City. This tragic event claimed the lives of over 1,500 people and revealed significant flaws in maritime safety practices and regulations, including lifeboat shortages and inadequate emergency protocols. Key figures involved in the Titanic's journey included Captain Edward Smith and J. Bruce Ismay, the managing director of the White Star Line, whose decisions during the voyage have been scrutinized in the wake of the disaster.

The Titanic struck an iceberg at approximately 11:40 PM on April 14, 1912, and sank in the early hours of the following day, marking a pivotal moment in maritime history. The ship, celebrated for its opulence and deemed 'unsinkable', became a tragic symbol of human hubris and the limitations of technology. The aftermath of the sinking led to the establishment of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) in 1914, which introduced stringent safety regulations for passenger ships, including lifeboat requirements for all passengers.

The legacy of the Titanic continues to resonate through history and popular culture, influencing countless works of literature, film, and art. The disaster raised awareness about the importance of maritime safety and contributed to changes in international maritime laws that prioritized passenger safety over corporate profit. In the years that followed, the Titanic's story prompted discussions about class disparities, as many of the wealthier passengers survived while most of the lower-class passengers perished.
